MN202611_1nyk85kd4me.t:
Whether it's scrolling through endless choice, spotting fake reviews, or working out if a "deal" is a deal at all, Black Friday sums up a lot of online woes.

Retailers promise bargains - but the sheer number of offers can leave us feeling no closer to finding the best deal.

It's an area where generative AI products, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini, have promised to help.

But are they any good at finding Black Friday deals? We had a go ourselves a week ahead of the big day.

Figures suggest relatively few UK shoppers currently go to AI tools for help.

A recent YouGov survey of 19 countries found the UK ranked second-last in the proportion of people who said they had used AI to help them shop.

Crucially, 36% of respondents who said they would be shopping around Black Friday didn't plan to use an AI tool at all.

But the survey suggested a growing number of people were considering it - and tech firms have released features to capitalise on this.

Amazon launched Alexa for Shopping for UK users in November and OpenAI launched a Shopping Research tool on ChatGPT days before last year's Black Friday.

In the US, Google recently launched Universal Cart, with AI-powered features such as price tracking and identification of relevant promo codes.

But there has been criticism that fact-checking AI ends up taking more time, while some brands are working to try to make sure their products show up in chatbot answers.

We asked four models to find a 55-inch TV deal, using the free versions of many of the most popular tools.

While this was not a rigorous scientific test, the experience we had produced mixed results.

OpenAI's ChatGPT came up with four options.

Its top pick was a Hisense TV on Chinese retailer Joybuy's website, on sale for £499 down from £649.

The next recommendation was a 55-inch TCL-branded TV, but a sidebar showed prices for the 50-inch version, from £379 to £814.

Option three was the same Hisense TV as before, but for full price at £649 from John Lewis and Richer Sounds.

This was the "best safer purchase" according to ChatGPT, as the sites offered longer guarantee periods.

But clicking on the links did not go well. Both retailers said the TV was no longer listed online.

The fourth option was equally fruitless - another TCL TV, at full price, £150 over our budget and not available online.

At the bottom, ChatGPT served one last offer - "one OLED option to compare" - for a £1,100 LG TV that was marked as "Ad" .

Claude produced the shortest answer of all the models we tested, and unlike the others, it did not give much detail on the specifications of each model.

Instead, it seemed to base its results on a small number of reviews published online.

It recommended the same two TCL TVs as ChatGPT.

But when we clicked on the links, they sent us to two dead pages on the Richer Sounds website.

Some other links led to year-old round-ups of Black Friday 2025 deals.

Claude was not very enthusiastic about its other two recommendations due to a lack of independent reviews - calling one "a decent option" but saying it "wouldn't pick" the other.

It also listed two Samsung TVs, but it told us not to buy them, with one "over budget and not clearly better than the TCLs".

We were left wondering why it even mentioned them in the first place.

Different AI model, same TV manufacturers - albeit different Hisense and TCL models to the previous chatbots' recommendations.

Gemini generated a table comparing four different models, but offered no links to the stores it named, so we searched for them ourselves.

The prices for one TCL TV were correct at £649, but it was sold out at one of the named retailers.

It said the other TCL model was available from Argos and Currys for £539 - correct for Argos, but when we checked Currys, it was £60 more expensive.

Again, it included two Samsung models to avoid due to lower screen specs.

Alexa came back with four TVs, from its own Amazon Ember at £532 to a £699 Samsung.

But its top recommendation was to go for another Samsung model at £616 (down from £749), based on its picture quality and Amazon customer rating.

Its fourth option was for a Sony TV, but it was only 50 inches, leaving us unsure why it had included it.

All the prices stated were correct, but Amazon only searches its own store. Alexa did acknowledge this, encouraging us to check its rivals for better deals, "as prices can vary" and we could get longer guarantees elsewhere.

There are methods that can boost the likelihood of getting a better response, from crafting more informative prompts to upping a chatbot's "thinking" level.

Tech journalist Alex Hughes had better luck than we did when he used ChatGPT's agentic AI mode to find a TV in last year's Black Friday sales.

Agentic AI is still in its early days, but it allows AI to act with more autonomy and carry out multi-step tasks.

The search took about 20 minutes "with very little work on my end needed," Hughes wrote for Tom's Guide , external in November 2025.

A year on, he told the BBC he didn't go through with buying a TV at that time.

He did later purchase one of the seven models ChatGPT had surfaced - but he had found it for a lower price in a bricks-and-mortar shop.

Will he be using AI to find Black Friday deals again this year? "Probably not," he said.

He reckoned it saved him time, but "when you're trying to deal with something like live price data... it will be inconsistent and quite often incorrect".

While we were served up the same brands again and again, in reality there are tonnes of products listed for sale around Black Friday.

Naureen Mohammed, who advises businesses on how to get their products to appear in AI results, told the BBC customers did not see the full picture when they talked to chatbots.

If businesses fail to update their prices when people start hunting for bargains, "last year's prices are served up as today's deals".

"I suspect the whole model for advertising is going to start influencing AI recommendations," she said.

Her own analysis of chatbots' Black Friday tech deals in the UK suggested the big retailers came out on top - with Amazon mentioned in half of responses, and Currys following closely behind.

Her tips include asking an assistant "is that this year's price?" and clicking on the links provided - "because you shouldn't take any advice from the AI system at face value".

But consumer group Which? recently said inaccurate pricing in AI results added more work , external to Black Friday deal-hunting.

"If you ask ChatGPT for a list of 10 laptops under £400 and seven of the results are priced higher, you've likely wasted a good chunk of time going through them to discover the bot gave you only three options," said senior researcher Hannah Walsh.

"The opposite is also true - you could miss out on great models in your budget if ChatGPT tells you they are more expensive than they actually are."

Avoid this Black Friday scam - how to check it's a real deal

MN202611_1af52eexyv8.t:
A separate 24-hour strike will begin on Monday morning as part of the same pay dispute

A 24-hour strike by resident doctors in Northern Ireland is due to end at 07:00 GMT on Saturday.

But consultants and specialist doctors will begin a separate 24-hour strike on Monday, as part of the same pay dispute.

The British Medical Association (BMA) rejected a recommended 3.5% pay rise and wants to restore the value of doctors' pay to 2008 levels.

Health Minister, Robbie Butler, said he had accepted the recommended rise but could not implement it without sufficient funding for his department.

Friday's strike action by resident doctors affected non-emergency services, resulting in the cancellation of many planned outpatient appointments.

Urgent surgery and most GP services continued as normal because senior doctors remained on duty.

Monday's walkout will involve consultants and specialty, associate specialist and specialist grade (SAS) doctors and will also take place over 24 hours from 07:00 on Monday.

Routine hospital and elective services are expected to be cancelled during the second strike.

But emergency care will continue under Christmas Day cover - which means full emergency cover will remain in place.

The Western and South Eastern health trusts have asked patients with appointments on Monday to attend as planned, unless their trust tells them otherwise.

The South Eastern Trust said the urgent care centre at Lagan Valley Hospital would be closed on Monday and that postponed appointments and procedures would be rescheduled as soon as possible.

Butler said more than 2,200 appointments were cancelled during similar strikes in June and warned the latest action would have "real consequences for patients, waiting lists and service delivery".

Scottish medic Dr Seamus Crumley said he had taken a pay cut to work in Northern Ireland

The BMA says years of below-inflation pay rises have made it harder for Northern Ireland's health service to recruit and retain doctors.

Dr Seamus Crumley, an anaesthetics registrar who works in intensive care at the Ulster Hospital, joined Friday's picket line in Belfast.

He told BBC News NI he had taken a pay cut when he moved from Scotland last year, despite securing a more senior role.

"The medical workforce here is very, very vulnerable to losing doctors to literally anywhere else in the UK, but also to the Republic of Ireland," he said.

Steven Montgomery says doctors face burnout due to pressure on them at work

Dr Steven Montgomery, who chairs the BMA's Northern Ireland Resident Doctors Committee, said his colleagues were facing burnout and emotional distress because of pressure at work.

He said the union was "not looking for this all to be paid in one lump sum" and wanted the minister to set out a plan to restore pay over time.

Dr Oisín Fearon, a resident doctor in Belfast, told BBC News NI he had considered moving to Australia, but family and local ties had kept him in Northern Ireland.

He said he had begun the process of registering to train in the Republic of Ireland and was keeping that option open.

Health Minister Robbie Butler introduced the Health and Social Care (Staffing) bill in the assembly on Monday

Butler said he had met the BMA to explain the financial pressures facing his department , external and intended to implement the recommended award as soon as possible.

He said cumulative pay rises over the previous three years averaged 30% for resident doctors, 25% for SAS doctors and 24% for consultants.

Butler said the recommended rise was higher than that for other healthcare staff and warned that going beyond 3.5% would have "significant repercussions for nurses, teachers, police officers and indeed the entire public sector workforce".

Separately, the Northern Ireland Public Service Alliance (Nipsa) released the results of a recent ballot of its health and social care members.

It said 94% of its health and social care members backed strike action, while 97% backed action short of a strike, over growing pressures on the health and social care sector.

The union said it would consider its next steps and warned that coordinated industrial action could spread across the health service in the coming weeks.

MN202611_80l88ie4pc.t:
Sales of a baby sleeping bag have been halted in the UK by fashion retail chain Next, after a new mum raised the alarm over its safety.

Emma Hunter, 29 from Norwich, contacted BBC Your Voice to say she realised the neck hole was far too big - meaning her daughter Rosie could potentially wriggle down, burying her face and risking suffocation.

Emma recalls: "I woke up my husband and we both agreed there was no way we could put Rosie in it."

Next says it's own-brand, 2.5 tog pink floral sleep bag with removable sleeves that comes in three sizes, has been removed from the website and stores and a product recall is underway.

Next will contact and advise customers who purchased the item from them.

The sleeping bag is now unavailable on Next's website after safety fears were raised

A spokesperson for Next said: "We can confirm the item has been removed from our website and all stores. A product recall is in place, and we are contacting all customers who purchased the item directly to advise them of the appropriate next steps."

Emma says she started doing her own research that same night she realised the sleeping bag was unsuitable for Rosie.

Although the product had a label stating that it met British standards, Emma discovered that the maximum neck circumference for that size of bag should be 32cm. When she measured the bag, the neck hole was 36cm.

According to the British Retail Consortium (BRC), a significant hazard arises if a child slips through the neck opening of a sleep bag and the material covers the child's nose and mouth.

They state that "suffocation can occur and may lead to the brain becoming starved of oxygen, which may result in asphyxia and potential brain damage or fatality."

To limit this hazard, the EN 16781 standard specifies a maximum and minimum size for the neck opening circumference in relation to the child's height.

For example, a sleep bag designed for a child 50 cm to 65 cm tall should have a minimum neck circumference of 28 cm and a maximum of 32 cm.

Rosie, who is now three and a half months old, measured 59cm at the time the bag was bought.

After flagging these issues to the company, Emma says she was surprised by their initial reaction.

"They seemed quite laissez faire about it and just offered me a refund, but I said 'it's dangerous, surely you shouldn't be selling it any more and there should be a product recall?'"

Emma was told by Next that they were looking into it and that their product team was examining the bag and would feed back.

Emma's older brother died of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome (SIDS) as a baby so the risk to babies from suffocation is something close to her heart.

She told the BBC: "I am more aware of this because of what happened to my brother and my family, but it shouldn't take an infant mortality to see change.

"They didn't have any sense of urgency about it at all and I expected a big high street store like that to have a certain standard. You put your trust into these retailers.

"How can a product have a label on it saying it met the British standard, when it clearly didn't?"

Ruth Watts, who is a qualified health visitor in England, says that babies will differ in terms of size and height, despite their age.

But if a sleeping bag covers the chin or face in any way, if it has a hood or no arms, it should not be used.

"The best thing to do is check the gap around the neck. If you can fit one to two fingers around the neck then that's safe. If it's any tighter or looser than that, then you shouldn't use it," she recommends.

Emma's baby Rosie is now 3 and a half months old and uses a different sleeping bag

The Lullaby Trust is a UK charity that works to prevent sudden, unexpected infant deaths, including SIDS.

CEO Jenny Ward told BBC News that the charity could not comment on the safety of specific products, since it does not carry out independent product safety testing.

But she encourages families to check that any product they use has passed the necessary safety checks and meets British Safety Standards.

She said: "Remember to follow the manufacturer's instructions and if a family is worried about any product we would say to stop using it and contact the manufacturer.

"We support the Office for Product Safety and Standards' recent warning on certain baby sleep bags and would urge families to ensure a sleep bag fits well before they use it."

People can check if any products have been recalled by visiting the OPSS website , external .

Online marketplaces still selling dozens of unsafe baby products, Which? finds

Calls for 'urgent action' on baby-sleep industry after BBC investigation

MN202611_f2ard43nty.t:
Perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, the notorious Rikers Island jail complex earned a variety of nicknames over the years

New York City's official overseeing the closure of the city's most notorious jail hopes a new plan from Mayor Zohran Mamdani will lead to "a moment of transformation" for how people are detained in the largest US city.

Mamdani on Friday unveiled a plan to close the Rikers Island complex by 2032, to build four new jails and drastically reduce the city's detainee population.

Plans to shutter the troubled facility date back to 2019, when the city council first voted to close it by this year. But plans have been delayed over the years in part due to the logistical difficulties over where to place inmates.

Dana Kaplan - who Mamdani appointed as the city's "Close Rikers Czar" told the BBC News channel on Friday that his latest proposal is not just about getting rid of a decrepit facility.

It is also a "generational opportunity" to "build a different type of detention system" and figure out how to detain people more appropriately, she said.

The Rikers Island jail complex is perched on a 413 acre (167 hectare) island between Queens and the Bronx, and has earned a variety of nicknames over the years because of its dilapidated conditions, including Gladiator School and Torture Island. The jail has housed a number of high-profile inmates awaiting trial, including Tupac Shakur, DMX and Harvey Weinstein.

It houses more than 6,500 inmates at a given time. Mamdani hopes to reduce that number to 4,100 - a goal that has been met with skepticism by the New York City correction officers' union.

"[B]uilding a new system that puts an arbitrary cap on the City's available jail beds is ill-conceived, irresponsible and jeopardizes the safety of all New Yorkers, including our Officers," NYC Correction Officers' Benevolent Association said in a statement. "The City cannot keep the jail population at around 4,100 without irresponsibly releasing individuals who committed violent felony charges."

"It's actually possible to have fewer people in jail in New York City - and that is what we should be planning for," she said.

The jail complex has long faced backlash over staffing shortages, crumbling conditions and inmate deaths in the facility, including nine this year. Legislation required the jail to be shuttered by 2027, but Mamdani blamed lags under former Mayor Eric Adams' administration as well as the Covid pandemic for the delays.

Last year, under Adams, a federal judge removed Rikers from the city's control, appointing an independent outside official to make decisions concerning the facility.

In an 88-page report released on Friday, Mamdani said Rikers was a product of "deteriorating infrastructure" and that officials had a "moral imperative" to close it.

New York City Council must approve the updated timeline, with members, including the city's speaker, indicating they support the plan.

Mamdani's office said the city would open up four new jails - one in Brooklyn by 2029, two in the Bronx and Queens by 2031 and one in Manhattan by 2032.

The mayor's office argues the new, smaller facilities will provide inmates "access to daylight, fresh air and clean space" leading to better outcomes for detainees. The facilities will be easier for families to access as well, as travel to the remote Rikers can take hours.

Mamdani said his administration would work to reduce the number of people being held in jail across New York City, including by offering alternative programmes to detention for some awaiting trial, by making it easier for families to post bail online and by trying to speed up the pretrial legal process.

He also wants to open up hundreds of beds in therapeutic housing units for prisoners with serious mental health issues.

Kaplan said Mamdani's administration had already opened 100 therapeutic beds at Bellevue Hospital in Manhattan, moving 100 people off of Rikers Island.

The proposal involves a large investments: $146m (£111m) for mental health and substance use treatment and vocational and education programming inside and outside the jails.

New York's infamous Rikers Island jail to close

'Gladiator School' - tales from NYC's notorious jail

MN202611_1ake0rp6x8j.t:
The ANC got the most votes overall but lost control in more than half of the councils it won in 2021

The party that has dominated South Africa for more than 30 years is in a race against time to secure power-sharing deals in most of the country's cities after a massive drop in its support in this month's local elections.

The African National Congress (ANC) suffered its worst result since it came to power in 1994 when South Africa transitioned from the racist apartheid system to democracy.

It won a majority in just one of the country's nine provinces, Limpopo, down from six in the last elections. It won the most votes in just two of the country's eight cities, compared with six in 2021.

At the national level, the ANC is sharing power with its long-time rival, the Democratic Alliance (DA), but while there is still no official announcement, it appears that ANC party officials do not want to replicate this at the local level.

Parties have until 27 November to negotiate and form local governments.

While the ANC saw a massive decline in its support, it still got more votes than any other party, 31%, down from the 46% in the last local election.

But in the country's economic powerhouse, Gauteng province, which includes Johannesburg and Pretoria, the picture is different. The pro-business DA got the most votes in both cities, as well as the province's other main region, Ekurhuleni.

Nationally, the party got 25% of the vote, up from 22% five years ago.

It also retained its majority in its power base of Cape Town, and got the most votes in Nelson Mandela Bay, where Gqeberha (Port Elizabeth) is located.

The left-leaning uMkhonto weSizwe (MK) Party, led by former President Jacob Zuma, came third, with 10% of the vote. This is a repeat of its performance in the 2024 national election, when it came in third and became the official opposition after the DA joined the coalition government.

It emerged as the biggest party in KwaZulu-Natal province, which includes the port city of Durban, securing 34% of the vote. However, this leaves it reliant on agreeing a coalition with other parties.

The only party to secure an overall majority in a city was the DA in Cape Town.

The DA and ANC have had an uneasy alliance since they entered a coalition, along with eight other political parties, in 2024.

The two, long-standing rivals due to their opposing policies, were forced into an agreement after the ANC lost its parliamentary majority for the first time since the end of apartheid. This became known as the Government of National Unity (GNU).

Despite this, the two parties have continued to disagree on key issues, and both sides have threatened to rip up their power-sharing deal.

Ahead of the local elections, analysts predicted that the two parties could team up at municipal level, mirroring the national arrangement.

ActionSA leader Herman Mashaba (left) and ANC chairperson Gwede Mantashe (right) look set to reach on agreement on co-governing some of South Africa's biggest cities

The ANC seems to have rejected this, with state broadcaster SABC reporting that most of the party's top leaders see an agreement with the DA as a last resort.

Instead, the party has been courting smaller parties to try and form councils in South Africa's cities.

In Gauteng, numerous reports point to an arrangement between the party and the anti-immigrant ActionSA, which emerged as the third largest party in the province with 17%, leaving it as a potential kingmaker.

The DA has also been trying to reach arrangements with smaller parties, and the ANC, but looks set to assume the opposition benches at least in Gauteng.

ActionSA is unlikely to work with the DA as they cannot agree on the mayoral candidates in Johannesburg and Pretoria.

It's too early to tell. Neither the ANC nor DA have spoken publicly about the future of their arrangement on a national level amid the ongoing coalition talks but the ANC's reluctance to partner with the DA in key cities points to continued strain between the two.

While the GNU has remained intact since it was formed in 2024, there have been those in the ANC who have been angered by what they view as the DA's dual role as opposition and partner in the coalition government and have pushed for the arrangement to end.

A party insider told the Daily Maverick on Sunday that a nationwide agreement to work with the DA at municipal level "was overwhelmingly rejected" at a meeting held by ANC members.

While some experts predict that the DA may have to consider its position in the coalition government given the ANC's stance, political analyst Andre Duvenhage told the BBC there was a possibility that "a lot of asymmetrical coalitions" could emerge - parties working together in one area and being in opposition elsewhere.

Another political analyst, Sandile Swana, said that any party wanting to leave the GNU over the failure to secure deals locally would be "[shooting] yourself in the foot".

The decline in the ANC's support was seen as being mainly due to high levels of corruption and a loss of confidence in its ability to provide basic services, such as electricity, water and rubbish collection.

While some attribute the increase backing for the DA to its record of competent management in municipalities under its control, some have accused it of neglecting poorer areas and townships.

But the experience of coalition governments over the past 10 years does not inspire much confidence that things will improve.

Half of the country's cities have been governed through power-sharing agreements since 2016 and these types of arrangements have often been viewed as unstable and chaotic.

As agreements collapse and new ones are forged, the delivery of basic services has often been affected.

This has been particularly evident in Gauteng, where governance in all three cities has come under scrutiny in recent years partly because of unstable governments.

Experts agree that even after new arrangements take effect, it will take longer than a five-year term to resolve the issues facing many municipalities, particularly South Africa's biggest city Johannesburg.

"I think if we are really turning the ship around, we are talking about a 10-year period," Duvenhage said.

Swana echoed this, saying it would take a decade to "cleanse and purify" local councils and "reinstate them as "proper municipalities".

ANC under pressure to reverse South Africa decline

South Africa's political marriage of convenience avoids divorce - just

'Devastating message' as ANC records worst-ever result in South Africa election

MN202611_jz869w6m7.t:
Mildred Juarez was stuck in detention for a month after her friends sent her bail money to Libre Immigration Services

Every morning for a month, Mildred Juarez woke up at five to be the first person in the showers at the immigration centre in Texas where she was being detained. Her friends had paid her bail, and she wanted to look presentable when she was finally released.

But every day, she was told her bond had not been paid.

Juarez was confused. Her friends had wired $2,600 (£1,970) to a bond company, Libre Immigration Services (LIS), that had been recommended by her lawyer. LIS said it would begin "the process of paying her immigration bond". But the next day came, and the day after that, with no release.

What she didn't know was that LIS was owned by a convicted fraudster, who had acquired the assets of another bail company co-founded by two men who also had fraud convictions. These two men were fined $811m in 2024 for scamming their clients.

Their firm, Libre By Nexus, which was at one point the largest immigration bail company in America, had appeared to shut down after federal regulators caught up with them.

But public records and BBC interviews with clients and former employees reveal a tangle of interconnected operations continued - along with the flow of cash - while leaving immigrants stuck in detention centres.

Since President Donald Trump has returned to office after promising an immigration crackdown, Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has made over 1.2m arrests, and fast-tracked deportations. The administration has tried unsuccessfully to make it illegal to give migrants bail but the sharp increase in detentions has increased demand for bond companies to secure bail and their release.

Conditions in these centres can be poor. Held in custody, away from family, often scared to speak out, many have faced health problems and endured inadequate food or treatment, according to immigrant advocates and reports by the US government.

"He did everything right" - The impact of Trump's immigration crackdown in Ohio

In the detention centre where Juarez was locked up, she and about 100 other detainees slept in bunks laid out in rows in a cacophonous room. The lights were left on all night and guards routinely woke everyone up for roll call. According to Castro and advocacy groups, detainees who caused trouble were put in "the hold" - solitary confinement.

The White House and officials from Homeland Security did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

For Juarez, the wait to be bailed out of detention seemed interminable.

In an email to the BBC, a spokesperson for LIS said Juarez "misunderstands" their services - that they are not bondsmen themselves, but they connect detained individuals to those who are licensed bondsmen. They said another company ultimately decided not to work with her.

An email sent by LIS, and reviewed by the BBC, said that the company had paid a cash bond to ICE on behalf of Juarez. The message was forwarded to Juarez as proof of payment a few days before her release.

But it was another bail agent, who was not affiliated with LIS, that got her out of detention - after her friends raised even more money to hire another company.

"I was losing it inside there," Juarez recalled, using an expletive.

"I lost everything. When I was released I had nightmares I was back inside."

Libre Immigration Services never paid back her deposit, despite sending messages promising a refund. A spokesperson told the BBC that they would refund Juarez's bail amount once her friend verified their details.

It is notoriously difficult for migrants like Juarez to make bail, which can be upwards of $7,000.

Once charged with illegal entry, a judge may grant bail, which allows the migrant to live freely while their case is heard, a process which can take years. Once a person's court case is completed, the bond amount is returned.

Bail agents, who are licensed to provide a down payment on bail and vouch that if the accused does not show up for court they will pay the rest, can help people get out of detention sooner. But many won't help migrants because they view them as too much of a flight risk. A 2024 government report found that a third of migrants not already in custody did not show up for court.

Libre by Nexus, also known as Nexus, was willing to take that risk.

Founded in 2013, its co-founders Michael Donovan and Richard Moore had served prison time in the 1990s and early 2000s for a string of fraud and forgery convictions.

Through his attorney, Donovan declined to comment. Moore did not respond to the BBC's request for comment.

Although people with felony convictions are barred from holding a bond licence in many states, Nexus operated as a kind of middleman between immigrant clients and licensed bondsmen.

Holed up in detention in Louisiana after crossing the border, Rosa Murillo heard about Libre by Nexus from another inmate, and the 18-year-old Honduran's mother called them to arrange her $7,000 bail.

A Nexus employee picked her up and took her to a hotel room where she was told she would have to pay $420 a month and wear a GPS ankle monitor until her case was completed.

Rosa Murillo says she was ashamed to wear the ankle bracelet that Nexus required

Federal regulators accused Nexus of implying, in their contracts, that the GPS bracelets were court-mandated, when they were actually the private company's requirement.

Murillo got a job as a waitress and tried to hide the ankle bracelet for fear that people might think she was a violent criminal.

Over the course of a decade, Libre by Nexus enabled more than 20,000 migrants like Murillo to be released on bail - and took in more than $230m in revenue, court documents show.

But the ankle bracelets were a constant source of annoyance for Nexus clients released from detention, according to two former employees who spoke to the BBC.

A former Nexus co-owner, Evan Ajin, told the BBC that the company stopped requiring released detainees to wear ankle bracelets in 2018.

When Mark Supetran worked for Libre by Nexus, he says he would tell people about how they had to wear an ankle bracelet

But Mark Supetran, who was based in the Philippines and worked for the company for a few months in 2022, says the bracelets were still in use when he worked for the company.

Supetran said he would field 80 calls a day from people who were either going through the process themselves or were the loved one of someone who was. Telling them they would have to wear a tag on release was part of the conversation.

"Part of the script was to say something like: 'The client will be wearing an ankle monitor.' So that got me thinking, like, why?" he recalled. "It doesn't make sense, we're not the government."

Not getting refunds of bail deposits was another complaint. Another former employee told the BBC he was instructed to tell callers that they would get their money back once their case was completed.

"But that that was never the case," he told the BBC. "I mean, you had people calling me in almost every day like 'Hey, am I gonna get my money back? Am I gonna get my money back?'"

Ajin, the former Nexus co-owner, told the BBC that the contract clearly stated that monthly fees did not go towards their bond, but were programme fees, and so they could issue no refund.

The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB), an agency created to stop predatory lending and other abusive financial practices, successfully sued Libre by Nexus and its parent company.

The lawsuit accused the firm of running a "predatory immigrant-services scam" that trapped victims into paying high, long-term fees. Nexus also misrepresented and concealed the terms, the lawsuit alleged, such as the non-refundable, monthly payments.

The judgment sided with the CFPB and a federal judge found the company liable for using predatory tactics against its clients in 2024, fining Nexus, its parent company, Ajin, Donovan and Moore $811m.

In addition to the hefty fine, the judge forbade the company from collecting on past debts.

Days after the 2024 order, Donovan sold a number of the company's assets, including customer lists and records - for $3.50.

As part of the agreement the buyer would also take on its debt.

Ajin says he ceased contact with everyone involved following the sale.

Moore is now in prison, after being convicted of filing fraudulent Nexus taxes. He and Donovan, who is also behind bars, are awaiting sentencing for insurance fraud and conspiracy. Donovan has also been charged with sexually abusing a boy under 12, but has not entered a plea in that case.

The purchaser of Nexus's assets was a Pennsylvania businessman named Vincent Smith, who had been sentenced to 10 months' probation in 2015 for conspiring with employees to write over $2m in fake bail bonds.

Smith called the new business Libre Immigration Services.

This March, the judge who issued the fine also ruled the sale of the company had violated her order by transferring the debts.

Judge Elizabeth Dillon voided the sale, but did not shut Libre Immigration Services down. She is due to review claims that LIS also violated the order by trying to build an app to collect debts from Nexus's old clients.

A former paralegal at Nexus, who went on to work for LIS, told the BBC about the app. She said after the sale, the lines between the two companies were blurred.

Another employee confirmed her account independently to the BBC, noting that the app was never finished because they could not obtain the client data.

A hearing date has not been set, and LIS has denied any wrongdoing, noting the company was never in possession of the client lists.

A screenshot of Libre Immigration Service's website

Libre Immigration Services continues to solicit immigrant clients and advertises its services online and on social media.

Its website features glossy photos of beaming families alongside the promise to "get your loved one released from a detention centre today!".

That wasn't Janie Aviles's experience. She had wired Libre Immigration Services $10,000 to help get her friend out of detention in Texas. But LIS did not pay his bail, Aviles said, until a month later, leaving him, like Juarez, in limbo.

When she called they offered various explanations and then stopped answering the telephone, she said.

Eventually she drove to the office listed on the website, which had shown a picture of LIS's logo hanging above the door. But on arrival, she found there was no storefront with the business's name and logo anywhere.

She said the company finally paid the bail a month after getting the funds, after she had reported them to the district attorney. No charges have been laid.

An LIS spokesperson said that "verification of significant information had to occur to prevent or minimise loss".

"The application was ultimately approved, and the cash bond was pledged to ICE. Presumably any delay related to the substantial bond amount and the heightened requirements of review."

They also said the office at that location was for business operations, and not client services, and that a sign had been ordered and would be installed, pending permits.

But the ordeal was enough to anger Aviles, who feared for her friend while he was stuck in detention. "I'm like 'This ain't right.'"

Ikaze mu kiganiro c'Imvo n'Imvano co kuri uyu wa gatandatu itariki 21 z'ukwezi kwa 11 mu 2026.

Mu ndwi iheze, ni ho sentare y'ishirahamwe ry'ibihugu vya Afrika y'ubuseruko yahimbaza imyaka 25 irangiye iyo sentare ishinzwe. Iyi sentare ifise icicaro i Arusha, mu buraruko bw'igihugu ca Tanzania, ahasanzwe icicaro gikuru c'iryo shirahamwe.

Igikorwa nyamukuru c'iyo sentare, ni ukwubahiriza amasezerano ashinga ishirahamwe ry'ibihugu vya Afrika y'ubuseruko no kuyashira mu bikorwa. Iraba kandi ko ibihugu bigize iryo shirahamwe, hamwe n'inzego zavyo, vyisunga amategeko.

Iryo shirahamwe ryatanguye ririmwo ibihugu bitatu, ubu ririmwo ibihugu umunani: Uburundi, Urwanda, Kenya, Tanzania, Uganda, Sudani y'Epfo, Republika ya Demokrasi ya Congo na Somalia.

Iyo sentare ifise n'akazi ko gutatura amatati yadutse hagati y'ibihugu bigize ishirahamwe rya Afrika y'ubuseruko, inzego zigize iryo shirahamwe, no hagati y'amareta y'ivyo bihugu n'abanyagihugu bavyo co kimwe n'amashirahamwe arangurira imirimo muri ako karere.

Mu vyo iyo sentare ishinzwe kandi, harimwo kuraba neza ko ibihugu bigize ishirahamwe vyubahiriza amategeko n'intwaro ibereye, gutyo ikagira uruhara mu gutsimbataza demokrasi muri ivyo bihugu.

N'aho igikorwa nyamukuru c'iyo sentare ya Afrika y'ubuseruko kwari ugukurikirana ko amasezerano ashiraho iryo shirahamwe yubahirizwa, kenshi na kenshi hari abayitura iyo bishitse amareta y'ibihugu bigize iryo shirahamwe agahonyanga uburenganzira bw'abanyagihugu

Kuva iyo sentare ishinzwe imaze guca imanza zirenga 1000.

Ego imanza ziracibwa. Ariko hari abidoga ko izo manza zidaheza ngo zishirwe mu ngiro.

Ikindi abantu bavuga, n'uko umwanya watanzwe kugira umunyagihugu wo mu karere ashatse kwitura iyo sentare ashikane ibirego vyiwe, ari muto. Ni imisi 60.

Hari abantu bamwe bamwe batazi ivyerekeye iyi sentare, uko ikora, ubwoko bw'imanza yakira ubwo ari bwo, uko bigenda mu kuyitura n'uko imanza yaciye zishirwa mu ngiro.

Ibi ni bimwe mu vyo tuza kwibandako muri iki kiganiro mwateguriwe kandi mugiye gushikirizwa na Cyriaque Muhawenayo.

Umutumire w'uyu musi n'umwe. Ni Kayobera Nestor arongoye sentare y'ishirahamwe ry'ubuseruko bwa Afrika.

Homes along Los Angeles' Sunset Boulevard could be seen engulfed in flames during the fires of January 2025

A jury in Los Angeles has found a 30-year-old man guilty of starting one of the most destructive wildfires in California's history.

Jonathan Rinderknecht was convicted of arson after starting the fires that swept through Pacific Palisades and parts of Malibu in January last year, killing 12 people and destroying more than 6,800 buildings in the US state.

The conviction was handed down nearly five months after deadlocked jurors led to the judge declaring a mistrial .

Rinderknecht, who had pleaded not guilty, was convicted of two federal charges. He is due to be sentenced on 17 March when he faces between five and 20 years in prison on each charge.

Jonathan Rinderknecht's arrest in October last year

Rinderknecht was found guilty of lighting a fire on 1 January last year which burned undetected deep in root systems before flaring back up six days later.

One of the charges was for starting the original brush fire, while the other centred on the damage caused when it reignited into a catastrophic blaze.

"We were determined to hold him accountable, and today's guilty verdict delivers a measure of justice for the families who lost loved ones and the thousands whose lives were upended," said Bill Essayli, who leads the US Attorney's Office for the Central District of California.

Rinderknecht is a Los Angeles resident and former ride-share delivery driver.

Defence attorney Steve Haney had argued at trial that prosecutors lacked sufficient physical evidence or records to prove their case.

Lawyers for the defendant said they were "disappointed" by the verdict but respected the jury's decision.

Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass, who was widely criticised for her handling of the fires, said in a statement that "no verdict can bring back the lives lost or erase the pain families have endured".

"So many are still struggling to rebuild," she said. "For those still displaced, the devastation remains a daily reality."

Prosecutors had argued that Rinderknecht was driven by revenge, anger and loneliness because he had nowhere to go for the holiday.

They cited geolocation data from his iPhone, security camera footage that showed his car's location and witness testimony from passengers.

They alleged that Rinderknecht had a "deeply entrenched belief that the wealthy were destroying the world" and in turn purposely started the blaze in the affluent neighbourhood.

The fire was one of several that ignited back-to-back across the LA region in January, which in total left 31 people dead and destroyed 16,000 structures.

Watch: Trump defends calling Putin a 'friend'

Ukraine's president Volodymyr Zelensky has labelled Vladimir Putin as a "killer" in response to Donald Trump referring to the Russian leader as his "friend" following their meeting in China this week.

Speaking to CNN, Zelensky said it was up to the US president "how to call Putin" but "for us, he is an enemy... for us, he's a killer".

On the sidelines of a historic trilateral meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Putin on Thursday, Trump called Putin his "friend" and said the two leaders have had a "great relationship for many years".

At least nine people were killed in Russian attacks targeting bridges in Kyiv and railway stations on Friday, days after Ukraine badly damaged the Crimean Bridge.

Zelensky called the attack the "biggest this year" and said the country suffered civilian deaths and injuries after an onslaught of 110 missiles, including 27 ballistic, and more than 400 drones.

Hours after the strikes on Ukraine, Trump told reporters at the White House that Putin would "love to end the war".

"They (Zelensky and Putin) both want to end it and it's a very good thing I have a relationship," he said on Friday.

Trump also doubled down on his description of the Russian leader as a friend but said he "can't speak" to whether Putin is a friend to the US.

However Zelensky said despite Trump's stance, he saw Putin as "a killer".

"I think mostly for the people in the world, he is a killer because he's killing - by the way- he's killing each day and night," he said.

Zelensky also said speaking about Putin like he is a "friend" means "he doesn't feel enough pressure".

The war of words came as Poland said a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.

Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.

Imibare mishya ijyanye n'ibyaha muri Afurika y'Epfo igaragaza ko abagore hafi 600 bishwe muri icyo gihugu hagati ya Nyakanga (7) na Nzeri (9) muri uyu mwaka.

Uyu mubare urimo abagore 13, imirambo yabo yasanzwe yambaye ubusa igice ndetse yakomeretse, ubwo yabonekaga ahantu rusange yari yajugunywe mu mujyi wa Johannesburg no mu nkengero zawo.

Ubwo bwicanyi bwateje uburakari bwinshi cyane mu gihugu ndetse polisi yotswa igitutu kugira ngo ishake ababukoze, muri icyo gihugu kiri mu bifite ikigero kiri hejuru cyane cy'ihohoterwa rishingiye ku gitsina n'ubwicanyi ku isi.

Mu bwicanyi buherutse kuba buteye ubwoba, muri iki cyumweru abagore batanu n'umwana w'igitambambuga bishwe barashwe mu ntara ya Free State.

Iyi mibare mishya ijyanye n'ibyaha, yatangajwe ku wa gatanu, yahishuye ko abagore 581 bishwe muri icyo gihugu hagati ya Nyakanga na Nzeri, barimo 131 biciwe mu ntara ya Gauteng irimo umujyi wa Johannesburg.

Iyo mibare yanahishuye ko habayeho igabanuka rito ry'umubare w'ubwicanyi.

Polisi yatangaje ko abantu 5,590 bose hamwe bishwe, abo bakaba baragabanutseho abantu 204 ugereranyije n'abishwe mu gihe nk'icyo mu mwaka ushize. Ariko ni ho ha handi ibyo bisobanuye ko muri rusange abantu hafi 60 bishwe buri munsi.

Ntibisobanutse niba uwo mubare w'abagore bishwe wariyongereye cyangwa waragabanutse kuko vuba aha polisi yari yararetse gutangaza iyo mibare kubera icyo polisi yavuze ko ari "inenge zikomeye" zari ziri mu mibare.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Minisitiri w'agateganyo ushinzwe polisi, Firoz Cachalia, yavuze ko bicyenewe ko habaho "ibikorwa byinshi cyane byo kwirinda... ihohoterwa" rikorerwa abagore n'abana.

Polisi ikorera mu ntara ya Free State, mu majyepfo ya Johannesburg, ivuga ko mu ijoro ryo ku wa gatatu abagabo batatu bipfutse mu maso barashe mu muryango utuye mu gace ka Botshabelo.

Polisi yavuze ko uko ari batatu bivugwa ko bari barimo bashaka nyir'inzu, nuko babonye ko adahari, "binjira mu nzu ku ngufu batangira kurasa abantu bari bayirimo".

Umugore wa nyir'iyo nzu na we yarashwe mu nda, ajyanwa ku bitaro. Nta bantu batawe muri yombi.

Ku wa kane, umukuru wa polisi mu ntara ya Gauteng yavuze ko abantu umunani bari bamaze gutabwa muri yombi bijyanye na ba bagore 13 bishwe, impfu zabo zigateza uburakari bwinshi mu gihugu muri uyu mwaka.

Jenerali (Gen) Tommy Mthombeni yavuze ko batatu muri abo batawe muri yombi bafashwe bijyanye n'iyicwa rya Elizabeth Moselakgomo, wakundaga gukora siporo yo kwiruka waburiwe irengero bigatuma habaho igikorwa cyo ku rwego rw'igihugu cyo kumushakisha, cyatangajwe cyane mu bitangazamakuru.

Uwo mugore wari ufite imyaka 38 yaburiwe irengero ubwo yari yagiye kwiruka nkuko yari asanzwe abikora buri munsi hafi y'urugo rwe ruri mu mujyi wa Kempton Park, mu ntara ya Gauteng.

Ku itariki ya 12 Nzeri, umurambo we wabonetse wakomeretse cyane ndetse igice cyawo ari cyo cyambaye imyenda.

Uwo mukuru wa polisi yavuze ko abandi bantu babiri bafunzwe bijyanye n'urupfu rwa Jabulile Ntimba, wari ufite imyaka 33, waje kuboneka igice kimwe cye cyambaye ubusa ndetse azingiye mu ishuka ari ku ruhande rw'umuhanda mu mujyi wa Boksburg, muri iyo ntara, ku itariki ya 17 Nzeri. Umurambo wa Ntimba wari uwa cyenda ubonetse mu karere ka Ekurhuleni.

Gen Mthombeni yavuze ko undi muntu yatawe muri yombi acyekwaho kugira uruhare muri bumwe mu bwicanyi bwabereye mu mujyi wa Kempton Park, mu gihe undi muntu ucyekwa yatawe muri yombi ashinjwa kugira uruhare mu rupfu rwa Ntombifuthi Nxumalo rwabereye i Tembisa, mu majyaruguru ashyira uburasirazuba uvuye rwagati mu mujyi wa Johannesburg.

Umurambo wa Nxumalo wasanzwe mu irimbi ku itariki ya 26 Nzeri. Yasanzwe yambaye ubusa, yakomeretse cyane ku mutwe, ndetse hafi y'umurambo we hari hari amabuye.

Undi muntu yatawe muri yombi muri Nyakanga, bijyanye n'urupfu rwa Busisiwe Mahlangu, umurambo we wasanzwe mu mujyi wa Kempton Park, ku itariki ya 15 Nyakanga. Umurambo we wari uwa mbere utahuwe, mu mirambo 13 yatahuwe muri ako gace.

Muri Nzeri, Perezida w'Afurika y'Epfo Cyril Ramaphosa yasezeranyije ko azakora ibishoboka byose kugira ngo abakoze ubwo bwicanyi bafatwe kandi baburyozwe.

Mu mwaka ushize, yatangaje ko ihohoterwa rikorerwa abagore ari "ikiza cyibasiye igihugu".

Ben White has made eight appearances for England.

Ben White's crucial goal against world champions Spain on Sunday will not be forgotten by England fans for a long time.

A smart finish to cap a flowing Three Lions move gave Thomas Tuchel's men an almost unbelievable 3-0 lead in Madrid . They hung on - just - meaning White will always be remembered as the player who scored that winner.

But, for White, the moment represented more than just a goal. It signalled a dramatic turnaround in fortunes for his international career - just four years after many thought his England days were over.

The Arsenal defender has had a tough time on the international stage to say the least.

He left the World Cup in 2022 after a disagreement with then assistant manager Steve Holland and made himself unavailable during the rest of Gareth Southgate's time in charge.

Since returning to England duty in March under Tuchel, the 29-year-old has now established himself as arguably England's best right-back - despite facing jeers from sections of his own fans for his decision to leave that camp.

The defender, who initially arrived at Arsenal from Brighton as a centre-back, has had an excellent start to the season, having played a crucial part in the Gunners' first title win for 22 years last time out.

It hasn't been straightforward for him at Arsenal either though. White has had to navigate his own injury problems and at one point when the defender was struggling for fitness, there was talk that the Gunners should look at moving him on.

But White has battled back and even dealt with competition from Jurrien Timber to remain one of Arsenal 's key players.

People don't know full story behind England exile - White

60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages

"I think just obviously people don't know the full story, because I never said anything and won't put anyone under the bus", White said before the England win over Spain.

The 29-year-old is keen to put the well-covered departure from the World Cup in Qatar behind him.

After his long absence from playing for England, some supporters did not believe that White should return.

His first appearance at Wembley since that incident in a friendly against Uruguay in March was booed by some supporters, loud enough for Tuchel to be asked about it after the match.

That game in itself was dramatic for White, who scored the opening goal for England before giving away the penalty that saw the Three Lions draw 1-1 with Uruguay.

White, who missed the World Cup with injury, had been expecting the reaction from some fans. But he is used to proving himself and changing the perception around him.

Tuchel was keen to back his player and said in the build-up to the Spain game that he hoped that the chapter was closed on White being booed by his own supporters.

"Obviously a bit tricky and not straightforward, but yes, it's obviously amazing to be here now." White said of his return to England.

White said in that same interview that he would make the same decision again that he did at the World Cup, but it was now time to move on.

His displays show exactly where his mindset is for his country.

He played the final 12 minutes in England's win over Croatia at Wembley before being brought into the starting line-up for England's toughest match of the November international break against Spain.

This new era of England is being dubbed Tuchel 2.0 and White firmly seems to be part of it.

Chelsea defender Reece James is out with injury. He is a big favourite of Tuchel's but cannot be relied upon for every game due to injuries.

White is a key player for the Premier League champions, reliable in defence and a threat in attack while being physically imposing. There is a lot for Tuchel to like.

And with three of his Arsenal team-mates on the pitch as England won the game, and Bukayo Saka to return, White brings the positives of the cohesion of a club side to Tuchel's team.

Arsenal supporters will not be surprised by White's excellent performances for England.

Since signing for the Gunners in 2021, not many players can say they have played more of a crucial role in Arsenal 's rebirth under Mikel Arteta.

Such is the importance of White, the Gunners attack does not flow as freely when he is not in the side to link up with Martin Odegaard and Saka as he relentlessly produces overlapping runs - a trait he showed when he scored England's third in Madrid.

His team-mates regularly say he is one of the fiercest competitors in training, and he has regularly shown his mentality when it looks as though things are going against him with his club side.

Arsenal signing Timber and a number of injury issues looked to have had White nearing an exit but, such is his determination, each time a challenge comes up he manages to turn it around.

White is a unique character within football, and has even said he doesn't watch the game away from the training ground, but his passion for his profession cannot be doubted.

Gunners fans will know that the level of passion he displayed in Madrid is something he shows every time he is on the pitch for his club side.

Watch: Miliband says tuition fees for EU students are a 'separate issue'

A deal agreed between the UK and the European Union on Friday will come into force regardless of whether the two sides can negotiate a separate tuition fees agreement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has told the BBC.

The measures agreed in Brussels include scrapping most checks on British food exports in return for the UK following some EU regulations from 2028, and a new youth mobility scheme.

However, a proposal from the bloc to lower the level of tuition fees paid by EU students in the UK has not been agreed.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she was "confident" a solution would be found, with Prime Minister Andy Burnham adding "me too" during a press conference announcing the deal.

Meanwhile, asked in his interview with the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether rejoining the EU would be looked at, Miliband said "all the options will be on the table".

It came after the prime minister said that he would discuss possible ideas for even closer ties with the bloc in the coming months.

What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?

Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow

UK and EU leaders have hailed the closer cooperation agreement, with Burnham calling the deal a "win-win" that could lower the cost of living and reduce red tape.

The prime minister said the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.

EU sources had earlier suggested that the bloc might hold up applying the wider deal until it was agreed that EU students who wanted to study in the UK would pay the same fees as British students.

Miliband said it was "absolutely clear" the agreements on food exports, energy and youth mobility would apply, even though there has not been a deal on tuition fees.

"President von der Leyen... was very clear about this at the press conference we just had. She said there are those three agreements and then there's a separate piece of paper and a separate issue, which is looking at the issue of tuition," he said.

Asked again whether the agreements would definitely become law, the foreign secretary said: "Yes, absolutely."

"The dates are set out in 2028 when these things are coming in, we're introducing legislation in Parliament, so definitely."

Miliband said there would be "no cost" to the UK taxpayer for anything agreed at Friday's summit, adding that there would be no new contributions to the EU budget.

He said previously announced agreements on EU schemes like Erasmus+ were a "separate decision" and the summit "was not about cost to the taxpayer".

Speaking on Friday, Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".

Miliband told the BBC that "of course all the options will be on the table" when pressed on whether rejoining the bloc would be considered, adding that "we will look at the benefits and the costs of all the different options".

He said that while he accepted the result of the 2016 Brexit referendum, "the world has changed massively".

"Europe is changing too, so we've got to look at what that means. It's not about this parliament, we're respecting the red lines in this parliament," he added.

Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal was "not fair", arguing that UK farmers would have to follow rules set in Brussels and young people from the EU would "compete" with young Britons struggling to get jobs at home.

She also claimed Burnham had "plucked" the £17bn figure out of thin air, and said the only modelling she had seen of how the agreement could boost the economy put the figure at "0.0%".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said Friday marked a "betrayal of the British people" and a good day for the EU to "try and humiliate" the UK.

Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, wrote on social media: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud."

Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.

"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."
